### Agent payment rails

**Verdict:** CONTEXT ONLY (watch) · **Cost:** No buyer fee · **Verified:** 2026-10-15 · 6 field(s) flagged ⚠

#### identity

**basics**

Not a shopping tool. These are the payment and identity layers that would let an AI agent pay on a person's behalf. (1) Visa Intelligent Commerce (VIC): Visa's umbrella for agent payments. It covers tokenised card credentials, Visa Payment Passkeys, the Trusted Agent Protocol (TAP) and Agent Directory, the Visa MCP Server, Intelligent Commerce Connect (pilot from 2026-04-09) and the Agentic Ready issuer programme (Europe from 2026-03-17). (2) Mastercard Agent Pay: 'agentic tokens' (scoped, tokenised credentials) plus payment passkeys and consent confirmation, with Verifiable Intent (an open SD-JWT delegation spec, draft v0.1) layered on top. (3) Web Bot Auth: an IETF draft, built on RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, that lets agents cryptographically sign their HTTP requests. Visa TAP builds on it, and Mastercard and Amex adopted it (Cloudflare, 2025-10-14). (4) BLIK agent-initiated payments: one pilot transaction (Juo chat agent at the Your KAYA shop, PayU acquiring, PLN 19.99, announced 2026-09-09) plus a PPRO-BLIK framework (announced 2026-08-12, exploratory). Role type: payment rail + protocol.

**vendor and ownership**

Visa Inc. (US) and Mastercard Inc. (US), card networks paid per transaction by the merchant side. Web Bot Auth: IETF Web Bot Auth working group. Its protocol draft is authored by T. Meunier (Cloudflare) and S. Major (Google). Cloudflare runs the 'signed agents' programme. BLIK: Polski Standard Platnosci sp. z o.o. (PSP), whose shareholders are Alior Bank, Millennium Bank, Erste Bank Polska, ING Bank Slaski, mBank, PKO Bank Polski and Mastercard (blik.com, 2026-09-09). Note that Mastercard is a BLIK shareholder. Pilot partners: Juo (Polish agentic-commerce startup, CEO Leszek Zawadzki), PayU (acquirer) and Your KAYA (cosmetics shop). PPRO: European local-payments infrastructure provider. Polish card issuers in the pilots: mBank, PKO BP (Visa), and mBank, Pekao, UniCredit (Mastercard). Merchant-side agents: in the Worldline/ING case the agent belonged to the merchant, not the shopper, which is a seller-side bias vector.

**lifecycle status**

Pilots and controlled live transactions only. No consumer product is available in Poland. Verified 2026-10-15. Timeline from primary pages: Cloudflare press release 2025-10-14 (Web Bot Auth for agentic commerce; Visa TAP built with Cloudflare; Mastercard Agent Pay and Amex adopt Web Bot Auth). The TAP sample repo was created 2025-10-10 and last pushed 2025-10-28. 2026-03-02: Santander + Mastercard, 'Europe's first live end-to-end payment executed by an AI agent', explicitly a pilot and not a commercial launch (search-result summary of the releases). 2026-03-05: Mastercard Verifiable Intent open-sourced (secondary). 2026-03-17: Visa Agentic Ready launched in Europe/UK. Phase one is issuer testing with 21 named issuers, none Polish (Visa UK release). 2026-05-25: Mastercard 'first authenticated agent transactions in Poland' with mBank, Pekao and UniCredit. A Mastercard test agent bought a coffee tasting in New York on Priceless.com, orchestrated by PayOS, as a pilot (bank.pl). 2026-06-02: Worldline + ING + Mastercard live end-to-end European agentic payment in production (NL) (Worldline release). Mastercard states that all its issuers in Europe are enabled for Agent Pay 'at a network level' (Mastercard perspective page via Glenbrook excerpt). 2026-07-02: Visa says 31 named European issuers, including mBank and PKO Bank Polski, completed live agent-executed transactions at lastminute.com, Frasers, Cleverbridge and BrickDepot, all secured with Visa Payment Passkeys (Visa UK release). 2026-08-12: PPRO-BLIK partnership, exploratory. 2026-09-09: BLIK first agent-initiated pilot transaction (blik.com). 2026-09: Web Bot Auth protocol draft adopted under the draft-ietf name (draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00, Standards Track, expires March 2027).

**cost model**

Buyer: no fee to pay by card or BLIK. Merchants pay interchange and acquirer fees. Card-scheme pricing for agent transactions is not published. Developer/merchant: Web Bot Auth is an open IETF draft, free to implement. Visa TAP sample code is free on GitHub (licence 'Other'). Visa MCP Server, VIC APIs and the Visa Acceptance Agent Toolkit need Visa Developer or Visa Acceptance credentials; sandbox sign-up is free, production terms are not published. Mastercard Agent Pay commercial terms not published. The BLIK agent-initiated service has no public pricing; it is a pilot. Seen 2026-10-15.

**⚠ feature geo matrix**

- **poland**: No consumer-available agent payment as of 2026-10-15. Visa: mBank and PKO BP are among the 31 issuers that completed live agent-executed transactions (2026-07-02), but neither has announced a customer product ⚠ *(unverified: bank pages not opened)*. Mastercard: pilot with mBank, Pekao and UniCredit (2026-05-25). Network-level enablement for all European issuers (2026-06-02) is an issuer-side switch, not consumer sign-up. BLIK: one pilot purchase at Your KAYA. The PPRO framework is exploratory with no launch date. Allegro: no agent-payment capability found.
- **eu**: Visa Agentic Ready: live transactions with 31 issuers in the UK and EU at four named merchants (2026-07-02). Mastercard: Santander pilot (ES, 2026-03-02), ING/Worldline production transaction (NL, 2026-06-02). All issuer- or merchant-controlled. No open consumer enrolment found.
- **us**: Mastercard Agent Pay launched first in the US with Citi and U.S. Bank cardholders (secondary coverage of the Santander release). Visa-OpenAI partnership announced 2026-06-10 (search-result summary). US-first pattern, as with other agentic checkout features.
- **language**: N/A - payment rails have no user interface. Language depends on the agent or merchant chat in front of them (the BLIK pilot ran in a Polish shop chat).
- **web bot auth agents**: Cloudflare's signed-agent cohort includes ChatGPT agent, Goose (Block), Browserbase and Anchor Browser. Claude's signing status is not confirmed ⚠ *(unverified)*. A local browser agent (Claude in Chrome, browser-use) does not sign requests by default ⚠ *(unverified)*.

#### capabilities

**spec and variant comparison**

N/A - payment rails carry no product or specification data.

**price comparison and pl coverage**

N/A - no price comparison. Polish merchant acceptance: the only named Polish merchant is Your KAYA (BLIK pilot). The Visa July 2026 merchant list has no Polish shop. No Allegro, Ceneo shop, Media Expert, x-kom or Decathlon.pl agent acceptance found.

**price history and omnibus**

N/A - payment layer only.

**⚠ total landed cost**

N/A - the rails do not compute shipping or returns. Relevant indirectly: Verifiable Intent constraints (amount bounds, budget caps) and the 'defined budget' in the ING case cap the total charged. A cap must therefore include delivery for a bulky item, or the purchase fails or needs re-approval ⚠ *(unverified: failure behaviour not documented)*.

**review and seller verification**

None for the buyer's purpose. The verification runs the other way: TAP, Agent Directory and Web Bot Auth let merchants verify agents and separate them from unverified bots. Mastercard says agents are onboarded within defined standards. Nothing in these rails checks a shop's identity, reviews or blocklist status for the shopper. Grade: none.

**safety and compliance checks**

N/A - no product safety or GPSR checks.

**independent test coverage**

N/A - not a product-research tool.

**alerts and monitoring**

The BLIK pilot is the one concrete monitoring pattern. The agent watched an out-of-stock variant and bought it on restock within prior consent (blik.com, 2026-09-09). Banks in the Mastercard PL pilot receive extended per-transaction data to monitor agent activity in real time (bank.pl). No consumer-facing price or restock alert product built on these rails was found.

**purchase automation and guardrails**

Yes. This is what the rails exist for, but no route is open to a Polish consumer today. Guardrails by rail: (a) Visa: a tokenised credential bound to the agent, Visa Payment Passkeys (biometric device authentication) on every transaction in Agentic Ready, consumer-defined parameters, and explicit cardholder authorisation. Visa claims this supports EU SCA. (b) Mastercard Agent Pay: agentic tokens that define the scope of the agent's permissions, payment passkeys (fingerprint, face or PIN) and consent confirmation (bank.pl, 2026-05-25). Verifiable Intent adds a signed delegation chain with 8 constraint types, including amount bounds, merchant allowlists, budget caps and recurrence terms (verifiableintent.dev, draft v0.1). In the ING/Worldline production case, the merchant's agent completed the purchase only after explicit consumer approval within a defined budget. (c) BLIK pilot: a prior instruction confirmed with a 6-digit BLIK code and a mandate approved in the banking app. At settlement no further tap was needed, and the agent stayed within user-set limits. Merchant of record: the merchant in every case (Your KAYA for BLIK). On error: card disputes follow normal chargeback rules, and Verifiable Intent is meant to speed dispute resolution. But who is liable when an agent buys the wrong item inside a valid mandate is legally unsettled under PSD2. SCA dynamic linking assumes a fixed amount and payee (Osborne Clarke analysis, search-result summary). BLIK said regulation, not technology, is the barrier (bank.pl interview, search summary). Claude Commerce Agents (Anthropic, 2026-09-09) has no charge method; checkout goes to the merchant or a payments partner.

**after sales and resale**

N/A for the rails. Recurring purchases and subscriptions are named as next use cases (Worldline release; Juo CEO in the BLIK release). That is relevant for consumables, not durables.

#### data and integration

**data sources and freshness**

N/A for product data. Status data comes from press releases by the networks, banks and PSP. Primary pages give exact dates. Much secondary coverage (stellagent.ai, ai2.work, paz.ai) restates releases, sometimes inaccurately. One summary said 'all cardholders' where Mastercard says 'all issuers ... at a network level'.

**⚠ api mcp skill access**

- **grade**: partial for developers and merchants; none for a buyer who wants an agent to pay from Claude Code
- **visa ai repo**: github.com/visa/ai - MIT, 45 stars, 20 forks, created 2025-11-05, last push 2026-09-30. Contains Claude Code skills (skills/ folder, copy into .claude/skills), a Gemini CLI extension, npm packages @visa/token-manager (JWE tokens for MCP auth), @visa/mcp-client and @visa/api-client (X-Pay auth, MLE encryption), a LangGraphJS 'vic-agent' demo (VTS tokenisation, FIDO device binding, Visa Payment Passkey creation, VIC enrolment), and a public documentation MCP server at https://sandbox.mcp.visa.com/mcp/doc (tool: get-docs). Live VIC access needs Visa developer onboarding.
- **visa mcp server and acceptance toolkit**: Visa MCP Server (VIC APIs) announced in pilot, September 2025 (corporate.visa.com, search summary). The Visa Acceptance Agent Toolkit runs as an MCP server for Claude Desktop or as a library (Vercel AI SDK). It needs Node 18+, a Visa Acceptance Merchant Organization ID (sandbox available) and REST shared-secret keys. It is merchant-side (invoices, payment links), not shopper spending.
- **trusted agent protocol**: github.com/visa/trusted-agent-protocol - licence 'Other', 213 stars, 45 forks, 19 open issues, created 2025-10-10, last push 2025-10-28 (nearly a year without code changes as of 2026-10-15). Sample stack: TAP agent (Streamlit, signs requests), merchant frontend (React) and backend (FastAPI, verifies signatures), CDN proxy (Node, RFC 9421 verification), agent registry (public keys). Spec page: developer.visa.com/capabilities/trusted-agent-protocol, 'available for use by merchants and independent developers'.
- **web bot auth**: IETF draft draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol (Signature-Agent header, JWKS key directory at a well-known URI). Cloudflare, Akamai and AWS WAF can verify signatures. Signing your own Claude Code browser agent would need your own key directory, and a merchant would still have to trust it ⚠ *(unverified: no consumer-agent registration path found)*.
- **mastercard**: Verifiable Intent spec and reference: github.com/agent-intent/verifiable-intent (Apache-2.0, draft v0.1). Agent Pay API specs and developer tools on Mastercard Developers are announced as 'to follow' (secondary). Agent Pay first offered to OpenClaw agents via Lobster.cash (secondary, not verified).
- **blik**: No public API for agent-initiated BLIK. Access only through pilot partners (Juo, PayU) or the future PPRO framework.
- **anthropic**: Claude Commerce Agents (2026-09-09): a merchant-side reference blueprint with a Claude Code plugin and GitHub repo. Visa and Mastercard are ecosystem partners, but the agent backend has no charge method (Crowdfund Insider).
- **setup effort**: Buyer: not possible today. Developer exploration: about half a day to run the TAP sample locally or connect the Visa docs MCP. No real payments without issuer and merchant onboarding.

**protocol support**

Visa TAP = Web Bot Auth + RFC 9421 message signatures plus Visa-specific consumer-recognition and payment fields (PAR for cards on file). Visa says TAP works alongside existing and emerging commerce protocols. Mastercard Agent Pay incorporates Web Bot Auth. Verifiable Intent publishes integration mappings for AP2, ACP and UCP. Amex uses Web Bot Auth. Implication: card rails are converging on Web Bot Auth for agent identity and on tokens plus passkeys for payment authority, so a future agent that signs requests and holds a scoped token should work across protocols. BLIK is the only A2A rail moving in (via PPRO), which matters because BLIK dominates Polish e-commerce.

**open source and licence**

Web Bot Auth: open IETF draft. Visa TAP sample: GitHub, licence 'Other', stale since 2025-10-28. visa/ai toolkit: MIT, active (last push 2026-09-30). Mastercard Verifiable Intent: Apache-2.0, draft v0.1. Mastercard Agent Pay, Visa VIC services and BLIK agent payments are closed.

**⚠ account linking and data access**

To use these rails a shopper would need: card tokenisation into the agent (Visa Token Service or a Mastercard agentic token) through the issuer, FIDO/passkey device binding, and consent per mandate. No raw card number reaches the agent. TAP passes consumer-recognition and payment identifiers (including Payment Account Reference) to the merchant. Issuers receive extended agent-transaction data. BLIK pilot: a logged-in shop account plus a banking-app mandate. GDPR: issuer, network and merchant are each controllers of their part. The agent platform also learns your purchase intent ⚠ *(unverified: data-sharing terms not published)*.

**automation legal risk**

For the buyer the legal risk is low; it sits with issuers and merchants. Practical point: signed agents (Web Bot Auth/TAP) are what merchants' bot managers will allowlist. Unsigned local agents may be blocked more over time (Visa: merchants decide whether and how far they admit agents). Regulatory: PSD2 SCA dynamic linking and liability for agent errors are unresolved. No EBA guidance on agent-initiated payments found (search-result summary of Osborne Clarke, March 2026). A UK consultation on agent payments closed 2026-10-06 (Bratby Law, search summary). BLIK/PSP calls regulation the main barrier.

#### trust and bias

**monetization and bias vector**

Networks and acquirers earn per transaction, paid by merchants, so their incentive is more agent-driven volume, not better choices. Bias enters (1) when the agent is the merchant's own agent (ING/Worldline case: the merchant's agent chose and curated the offer), (2) through merchant agent-allowlisting, which decides which shops an agent can even transact with, and (3) through Claude Commerce Agents, which are also merchant-side. These rails do not rank products, so no sponsored-results issue arises at this layer.

**ranking transparency**

N/A - no ranking. Positive for auditability: Verifiable Intent produces a tamper-evident record of who authorised what within which bounds.

**run to run consistency**

N/A - deterministic payment rails. The agent choosing what to buy above them is not deterministic (see ACES, Wharton and Product.ai evidence).

**manipulation and injection resistance**

The rails limit damage, not persuasion. Scoped tokens, amount bounds, merchant allowlists and passkey confirmation stop an injected agent from paying an arbitrary payee or amount. They do not stop an agent from being talked into a worse product inside its limits. Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace (Nov 2025, synthetic markets) reported payments redirected to malicious agents for some models (search-result summary, not re-opened). TAP helps merchants exclude bad bots. It does not help a shopper's agent avoid fake shops.

**known failures**

No public failure reports, because volumes are tiny: one transaction each for Santander, ING/Worldline, the Mastercard PL pilot and BLIK. Recurring problems are in communication: competing 'Europe's first' claims, trade coverage turning 'issuers enabled at network level' into 'all cardholders', and conflicting details about what was bought (gift search vs concert tickets). Cloudflare's Agents SDK integration was announced in October 2025 as coming 'soon'; delivery not confirmed. The TAP sample repo has had no commits since 2025-10-28 and has 19 open issues. Columnist skepticism in Poland: 'more announcing than deploying' (xyz.pl, search summary).

**regulatory enforcement history**

N/A - no regulatory decisions specific to these agent-payment programmes found. Open regulatory questions (PSD2/PSR SCA, liability) are noted under automation_legal_risk.

**⚠ buyer protection path**

Card rails: the merchant stays merchant of record. The 14-day withdrawal right and statutory warranty (rekojmia) apply against the merchant as usual. A card chargeback goes through the issuer. Verifiable Intent aims to make agent disputes evidence-based. Open risk: if the agent bought within a valid mandate, the payment may count as authorised, which weakens the 'unauthorised transaction' refund route ⚠ *(unverified: no ruling or EBA guidance found)*. BLIK: an account-to-account payment with no card-style chargeback. Disputes go to the merchant or PayU, and unauthorised-payment claims to your bank ⚠ *(unverified: BLIK dispute rules for agent payments not published)*.

#### fit for user

**fit for big ticket durables**

Low today, and should stay human-confirmed. For a ~3 m trampoline (about EUR 200-700) none of these rails can be used from Poland now. Even once they are, the sensible pattern is: the research agent produces the shortlist and evidence, you pick, and payment needs a per-transaction passkey or BLIK confirmation with a hard cap (for example the chosen offer price plus delivery) and a single-merchant allowlist. The one agent-pays scenario that fits durables is the BLIK-style 'buy when back in stock or below price X at shop Y, within a cap' mandate. That is useful for a specific trampoline model on a Decathlon.pl or Allegro listing, but only once Polish merchants accept agent payments.

**workflow role**

Purchase step only (plus restock- or price-triggered purchase). For now, context only: design the buying skill to stop at a cart or checkout link and leave payment to the human. Combine with the research and price-tracking tools upstream.

**effort and cost per purchase**

Buyer: 0 PLN in payment fees, but not available. Developer experimentation: about 4-8 hours to run the Visa TAP sample or wire the Visa docs MCP into Claude Code, with no per-query fees and no real purchase possible without onboarding. No arithmetic per comparison applies, since the rails do no research.

**evidence trail**

Future agent payments would leave a strong trail: a Verifiable Intent SD-JWT chain (identity -> intent -> action), issuer transaction data, and banking-app confirmations (BLIK). Today the only saveable evidence is the announcements. Suggested vault record for any future agent purchase: mandate parameters (cap, merchant allowlist, expiry), merchant, amount incl. delivery, token or card last 4, approval timestamp and method (passkey/BLIK), order number, and the research note that justified the pick.

#### assessment

**strengths weaknesses**

- **strengths**:
  - Strong guardrail design: scoped tokens, per-transaction passkeys or BLIK confirmation, amount and merchant constraints (Visa release 2026-07-02; Verifiable Intent draft v0.1; BLIK pilot).
  - Polish banks are already in the pilots (mBank and PKO BP with Visa; mBank, Pekao and UniCredit with Mastercard), so PL availability is plausible next.
  - BLIK, the dominant Polish online payment method, is building agent-initiated payments (PPRO 2026-08-12, pilot 2026-09-09).
  - Open building blocks exist: Web Bot Auth IETF draft, TAP sample code, Verifiable Intent (Apache-2.0), Visa's MIT toolkit with Claude Code skills.
- **weaknesses**:
  - No consumer access in Poland as of 2026-10-15. Everything is pilot or controlled live transactions.
  - Nothing here helps verify a product, a shop or a price. It only moves money once the choice is made.
  - Liability for agent mistakes inside a valid mandate is legally unsettled (PSD2 SCA dynamic linking, no EBA guidance found).
  - Developer access is merchant- or issuer-oriented. There is no shopper-side API for a Claude Code agent to hold a scoped payment token.
  - Merchant-side agents (ING/Worldline, Claude Commerce Agents) put the seller's agent in charge of choosing, which is a bias vector.

**independent review consensus**

No independent hands-on evidence found. All transaction claims come from Visa, Mastercard, banks, Worldline, BLIK or PPRO releases and trade press that restates them. Independent analysis is legal commentary on PSD2/SCA and liability (Osborne Clarke, Bratby Law; search-result summaries) and Polish skepticism that deployment lags announcements (xyz.pl). The consensus in that commentary: the technology is ready, while regulation and liability are not.

**verdict for me**

CONTEXT ONLY (watch). Deciding fact: as of 2026-10-15 there is no consumer-available agent payment in Poland. The PL items are pilots (Mastercard 2026-05-25, Visa issuers mBank/PKO 2026-07-02, BLIK 2026-09-09). Best use: keep payment manual and have the buying skill stop at a checkout link. Re-check in six months whether mBank or PKO BP offer agent tokens with per-transaction passkeys and caps.

**⚠ conflicting evidence**

- 'Europe's first live agent payment': Santander + Mastercard claimed it on 2026-03-02, and Worldline + ING claimed 'Europe's first end-to-end agentic payment in production' on 2026-06-02. The difference is pilot vs production framing.
- Scope of Mastercard enablement: Mastercard says all European issuers are enabled 'at a network level' (2026-06-02). Some secondary coverage implies all cardholders can use it. No source confirms consumer enrolment.
- Visa issuer counts: 21 named issuers in Agentic Ready phase one with no Polish banks (2026-03-17), versus 'over 30' and 31 named issuers including mBank and PKO BP with live transactions (2026-07-02). Different programme stages.
- What was bought in the ING case: the Worldline release describes an anniversary-gift search where the agent found concert tickets. Other coverage says tickets for a named orchestra. Core facts agree.
- BLIK share of Polish e-commerce: PPRO (2026-08-12) says about 71% of e-commerce transactions, a figure The Paypers attributes to cashless.pl, with no period stated. A secondary source cites NBP data of about 70% by volume for Q1 2025. PSP has estimated 70%. BLIK's 2023 report says 50% market share. The 48% figure is e-commerce's share of BLIK's own volume (2025), a different measure. The task note's 'Q4 2025' period for 71% could not be confirmed ⚠ *(unverified)*.
- Santander pilot details: official releases describe a controlled pilot with no product named. Stellagent says a T-shirt purchase in Spain (unverified).

## G. Savings add-ons

### Cashback and coupon tools

**Verdict:** PILOT (minor add-on) · **Cost:** Free, shop-funded · **Verified:** 2026-10-15 · 12 field(s) flagged ⚠

#### identity

**basics**

Affiliate-funded savings add-ons that pay back part of the shop's commission or apply coupon codes. (1) PayPal Honey: coupon-finder browser extension with Honey Gold rewards, US/UK-centric. (2) goodie: Polish cashback, coupon and leaflet app/website with about 800 shops (vendor-claimed). (3) LetyShops: cashback portal and extension with 3,046 shops in its Polish listing (vendor-claimed). (4) AleRabat (alerabat.com): Polish coupon site with an auto-apply extension and cashback, about 1,500 shops (secondary review). (5) PAYBACK Polska: multi-partner loyalty points (100 points = 1 PLN) in store and online. (6) Bank-card cashback: card-level percentage back, usually capped monthly. None compares products or prices. Role type: coupon/cashback tool (affiliate intermediary).

**⚠ vendor and ownership**

- **honey**: Honey Science Corporation (PayPal Honey), Los Angeles. A PayPal subsidiary since its 2020 acquisition for about USD 4B (Wikipedia).
- **goodie**: Millennium Goodie sp. z o.o., Warsaw (goodie.pl footer), a Bank Millennium company. Since 2025-11-27 the bank's in-app 'Zwroty za zakupy' cashback programme is organised by Bank Millennium SA itself, with goodie running the platform (bezprawnik.pl, search-result summary). Bank ownership means cross-selling of Millennium products and eKarty prepaid cards.
- **letyshops**: Letyshops KFT, Csomad, Hungary (letyshops.com/pl footer). Founded in Ukraine in 2014 by Igor Gnatovsky. One German source calls it a subsidiary of Lety Group AG (Switzerland) ⚠ *(unverified: secondary)*. Received USD 3M in 2020 from AB Capital, owner of the Admitad affiliate network (secondary).
- **alerabat**: Alerabat.com sp. z o.o., ul. Fabryczna 22, Katowice, KRS 0000570132, share capital PLN 30,000 (alerabat.com/regulamin).
- **payback**: PAYBACK, part of Management Holding Loyalty Partner GmbH in the American Express Group (payback.group). Polish programme launched 2009. Polish operating entity not named on payback.pl ⚠ *(unverified)*.
- **bias note**: Every operator earns affiliate commission from the shops it lists. Goodie is bank-owned and Payback is Amex-owned. None is a neutral price tool.

**lifecycle status**

All active as of 2026-10-15. Honey is damaged: Google announced a Chrome Web Store affiliate-ads policy on 2025-03-11 and began enforcing it on 2025-06-10. MegaLag investigations followed (December 2024, then 2025-12-21 and 2025-12-30). Rakuten Advertising terminated Honey on 2026-01-12, impact.com suspended it on 2026-01-16, and Awin suspended payments and new-programme access on 2026-01-21. PayPal said it disabled the flagged code in mid-January 2026. Rakuten reportedly reinstated Honey in May 2026 (ppc.land, 2026-08-11, secondary). The creator class action (N.D. Cal.) was dismissed with leave to amend in November 2025 and refiled in January 2026. On 2026-06-22 the renewed motion to dismiss was denied and the case moved into discovery (ppc.land). goodie: live (homepage 2026-10-15); bank-programme organiser changed 2025-11-27. LetyShops: live, '12 years of operation', (c) 2014-2026. AleRabat: live, added in-store cashback in 2025 (android.com.pl, secondary). PAYBACK PL: live. A German point expiry on 2026-09-30 applies to Germany; not confirmed for Poland.

**⚠ cost model**

Free for users. Funded by shop commissions. AleRabat says it passes on 50-80% of the commission. Payout thresholds: goodie minimum 21 PLN, bank transfer (goodie.pl). AleRabat minimum 50 PLN to a bank account (android.com.pl review, secondary) ⚠ *(unverified)*. LetyShops: PayPal, SEPA transfer or bank account; minimum not shown on the homepage ⚠ *(unverified)*. PAYBACK: 100 points = 1 PLN, no minimum payout threshold (payback.pl). Honey: Honey Gold points redeemable for gift cards. Bank cards: up to about 0.5-1.5% flat, or 5% in categories with 50-100 PLN monthly caps. These figures come from freenance.io, an inconsistent ranking site, and were not verified on bank pages ⚠ *(unverified)*. Seen 2026-10-15, PLN.

**⚠ feature geo matrix**

- **poland**: goodie, LetyShops, AleRabat, PAYBACK: Polish-language sites and apps for Polish shops. Honey: Poland is not listed as a supported market (Honey help centre names US, CA, AU, UK 'and more'; the 2021 EU launch covered DE, NL, ES, IT, FR). Not confirmed for Poland.
- **eu cross border**: LetyShops lists Amazon PL and runs 30+ country sites. Whether a Polish account earns cashback on Amazon.de is not confirmed. Honey may work on Amazon.de and German shops ⚠ *(unverified: not tested)*. PAYBACK PL lists 'Amazon' as an online partner (likely amazon.pl) ⚠ *(unverified)*; the German PAYBACK programme is separate.
- **us**: Honey is US-first (most merchants and features).
- **language**: Polish UI for goodie, LetyShops PL, AleRabat and PAYBACK PL. Honey in English and other languages, no Polish shop coverage confirmed.

#### capabilities

**spec and variant comparison**

None. These tools work at shop level, not product level. No spec, EAN or variant mapping.

**price comparison and pl coverage**

No price comparison across shops. Shop coverage (vendor-claimed unless noted): goodie about 800 shops, featuring Allegro (standard up to 2.2%, temporary boost up to 20% until 2026-10-19), AliExpress, Temu and Amazon. LetyShops 3,046 shops, including Allegro (1.7-5.1%), Decathlon PL (2.25%), Amazon PL (up to 5-15%) and MediaMarkt (up to 3.5-10.5%). No Media Expert listing seen. AleRabat about 1,500 shops (secondary review, 'thousands' elsewhere). PAYBACK: about 300 online brands (bank.pl, undated) or 350+ partners (app listing). Named online partners include Amazon, RTV EURO AGD and Carrefour. Decathlon, Leroy Merlin, OBI, Castorama, Media Expert and Allegro were not seen on payback.pl. Rates are 'up to' and depend on category. Not tested.

**⚠ price history and omnibus**

None in the Polish tools. Honey historically offered Amazon price history and a 'Droplist' price watch ⚠ *(unverified: not verified as current)*. No tool shows the Omnibus 30-day lowest price or flags fake discounts. Risk: a boosted cashback rate can pull you to a shop whose price is higher than elsewhere.

**total landed cost**

No. They make it worse to reason about: LetyShops calculates cashback on the net value excluding VAT, other taxes and delivery (Decathlon PL shop page). The effective rate on the gross price is therefore about 1/1.23 of the headline. Returns cancel cashback or points (LetyShops; payback.pl). Shipping and return fees are not included.

**review and seller verification**

None. Shops are whoever has an affiliate agreement. Listing implies only that the shop pays commission. Grade: none.

**safety and compliance checks**

None.

**independent test coverage**

None. They do not surface lab tests.

**⚠ alerts and monitoring**

Boosted-rate offers are promoted in the apps, and LetyShops runs time-limited 'hot cashback'. Push-alert behaviour not verified ⚠ *(unverified)*. GotCashback (third-party MCP, see api_mcp_skill_access) offers cashback-rate alerts after sign-in. No price-drop or restock alerts for Polish shop pages. Honey Droplist status unverified ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**purchase automation and guardrails**

No purchasing. The AleRabat and Honey extensions auto-apply coupon codes in the cart. AleRabat markets this as 'save automatically in the basket'. No payment credentials are involved. Under Chrome Web Store policy (enforced 2025-06-10), an extension may inject affiliate links or cookies only after a user action and only when it gives a real discount or cashback at that moment.

**after sales and resale**

Brief: returns within the shop's return window cancel cashback or points. Cashback is credited only after that window, which is why confirmation takes 60-90 days or more. No spare-parts or resale features.

#### data and integration

**data sources and freshness**

Affiliate-network transaction reports, which the shop must confirm, plus coupon databases. LetyShops Decathlon: pending within 1 day, confirmed in 60-90 days, and a missing-cashback claim must be filed within 3 months (shop page). An Allegro forum moderator, citing the partner, said 75-150 days for LetyShops via Allegro (search summary). An older Pepper post reported 3-4 months. Goodie: points from unconfirmed transactions expired after 6 months under older terms (Pepper quote, search summary). Honey's coupon database fell from about 90,000 to about 50,000 codes, with at least 10,000 reported expired (ppc.land, citing a video investigation).

**⚠ api mcp skill access**

- **grade**: partial (rate comparison only, via a third-party MCP); none for the individual portals
- **official apis**: No public API or official MCP found for goodie, LetyShops, AleRabat, PAYBACK or Honey (search 2026-10-15).
- **gotcashback mcp**: GotCashback (MNP Enterprises, LLC, founded 2020) runs a remote MCP server at https://mcp.gotcashback.com (Streamable HTTP). It has 18 tools: 12 comparison tools with no sign-in, such as cashback rates by store name and country, gift-card discounts and portal lookup, and 6 account tools (favourites, alerts) via OAuth 2.1. The REST API is described as free with no key. Covers 42 countries and 113 portals. Poland is included (gotcashback.pl): 12 Polish portals and about 3,470 stores, named portals AleRabat, Tipli.pl, SimplyBestCoupons.pl, ShopBuddies.pl, Bonusway.pl and CashGoback.pl. goodie, LetyShops and PAYBACK are not named ⚠ *(unverified: whether covered)*. Example: Allegro up to 2.15% (SimplyBestCoupons.pl) on 2026-10-15. Add with: claude mcp add --transport http gotcashback https://mcp.gotcashback.com. Affiliate disclosure exists but was not read.
- **browser agent**: Possible but counter-productive. Cashback depends on a clean cookie path (clear cookies, click through the portal, buy in the browser, not the shop's app). An automated agent doing this can lose attribution or look like fraud. Use manually.
- **setup effort**: About 5 minutes to add GotCashback MCP. About 10-20 minutes per portal account. Then about 2-3 minutes manual work per purchase.

**protocol support**

None. No ACP, UCP, AP2 or MCP support from the portals themselves. MCP access exists only through the third-party GotCashback aggregator.

**open source and licence**

Closed (Honey, goodie, LetyShops, AleRabat, PAYBACK, GotCashback).

**⚠ account linking and data access**

Account needed: e-mail, or Google, Facebook or Apple login. On AleRabat, social login makes your name and photo public on the site (regulamin). Payout needs an IBAN or PayPal. Browser extensions need broad page-access permissions to detect shops and apply codes ⚠ *(unverified: exact permissions not reviewed per extension)*. Honey: Amazon warned users in 2019 that it was a privacy risk, and the December 2025 MegaLag video alleged collection of personal data beyond shopping (Wikipedia). goodie is part of the Bank Millennium group and PAYBACK profiles purchases across partners for personalised coupons ⚠ *(unverified: data-sharing scope not read in privacy policies)*. GDPR applies to the Polish and Hungarian operators. Honey is a US company.

**⚠ automation legal risk**

Low for normal manual use. Risks: running several cashback or coupon extensions at once overwrites each other's last-click cookies, causing rejected cashback. Honey's alleged affiliate-link hijacking is the extreme case. Multiple accounts lead to blocked payouts (a goodie user reported a payout blocked for 'more than one account', search summary). Scripted click-throughs likely breach portal terms ⚠ *(unverified: ToS not read)*.

#### trust and bias

**⚠ monetization and bias vector**

Pure affiliate economics. Cashback is a share of the shop's commission (AleRabat: 50-80%). Bias vectors: (1) coverage bias, since only commission-paying shops appear; (2) boosted rates steering you to particular shops (goodie Allegro up to 20% for a week); (3) Honey: PayPal says merchants decide which coupons appear (Wikipedia), and Honey was accused of replacing creators' affiliate links; (4) the bank owner (goodie/Millennium) and Amex (PAYBACK) cross-sell financial products. Paid placement in the featured-shop lists is not disclosed ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**ranking transparency**

Low. Featured-shop lists and 'up to' rates without the category breakdown up front. Rates change daily (GotCashback says rates older than 24 hours are stale). No explanation of ordering.

**run to run consistency**

N/A - non-AI tools.

**manipulation and injection resistance**

N/A for AI. Practical risks: expired or fake coupon codes (Honey's database decay) and look-alike coupon sites. The Chrome policy limits silent affiliate injection, but enforcement against specific extensions has not been documented publicly.

**known failures**

Rejected or untracked cashback is the main complaint. A goodie Decathlon bike cashback was rejected, then paid after Decathlon confirmed the order on the user's request (Pepper/forum, search summary). LetyShops Decathlon page rating is 3.40/5 from 43 reviews, with several missing-cashback reports. LetyShops Firefox add-on: 3.53/5 from 245 reviews. Slow confirmation: 60-150 days. App purchases are not tracked (LetyShops Decathlon; PAYBACK online). Payouts blocked over alleged duplicate accounts. Users say goodie rates are lower than competitors (forum anecdotes). Honey: affiliate-network removals and coupon-database decay. Most forum evidence is from 2021-2025 and is anecdotal.

**⚠ regulatory enforcement history**

Honey: In re PayPal Honey Browser Extension Litigation (N.D. Cal.), creator class action in discovery after the 2026-06-22 ruling. No liability finding and no class certified. Separate GamersNexus suit filed 2025-01-03. Chrome Web Store affiliate policy change (2025) followed the controversy. Goodie, LetyShops, AleRabat, PAYBACK: no UOKiK decision found. A Pepper thread is titled 'Nieuczciwe praktyki Goodie a UOKiK', but its content could not be loaded ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**⚠ buyer protection path**

Unchanged. You buy directly from the shop, which is merchant of record. The 14-day withdrawal right, statutory warranty (rekojmia) and card chargeback or PayPal protection apply as usual. Cashback is a separate promise from the portal under its own terms. A cashback dispute goes to goodie (Polish company), LetyShops (Hungarian KFT; cross-border, ECC Poland route possible ⚠ *(unverified)*) or AleRabat (Polish company). Using the withdrawal right cancels the cashback.

#### fit for user

**⚠ fit for big ticket durables**

Low value, low effort. Worked example for a ~3 m trampoline at 1,800 PLN gross: LetyShops Decathlon 2.25% on the net value excluding VAT and delivery gives 1,800 / 1.23 x 2.25% = about 33 PLN, credited 60-90 days later and lost if returned or untracked. goodie on Allegro at the standard 'up to 2.2%' gives at most about 40 PLN (category rate may be lower). PAYBACK at a partner earning 1 point per 3 PLN (Carrefour rate) gives 600 points = 6 PLN, if the shop is a partner at all ⚠ *(unverified)*. A 1.5% card cashback gives about 27 PLN, within monthly caps (unverified). By contrast, a 5% price difference between two shops for the same model is 90 PLN, so shop choice by landed price dominates. Cashback should only break ties.

**workflow role**

The last step before paying, after the shop and offer are chosen: check whether the chosen shop has cashback or a coupon (GotCashback MCP can query rates across Polish portals), click through one portal only, then buy. Never let cashback pick the shop. Combine with Ceneo or price-history tools upstream.

**effort and cost per purchase**

0 PLN. Setup about 10-20 minutes per portal account, plus about 5 minutes for the GotCashback MCP. Per purchase about 2-3 minutes (rate check, clear cookies, click through, buy in a browser). Then wait 2-5 months and possibly file a claim. Arithmetic for one comparison: one GotCashback call per candidate shop, for example 3 shops = 3 tool calls and a few thousand tokens.

**evidence trail**

Portal account history shows pending, confirmed and rejected statuses. GotCashback answers carry a rate timestamp. Vault record to keep: portal, shop, rate and its date, order number and date, gross and net amount, expected cashback, claim deadline (LetyShops: 3 months), payout date. Needed because claims require order evidence.

#### assessment

**strengths weaknesses**

- **strengths**:
  - Free and wide Polish shop coverage: about 800 (goodie), 3,046 (LetyShops), about 1,500 (AleRabat), all vendor-claimed.
  - Cash payouts with low thresholds: goodie 21 PLN, PAYBACK no minimum at 100 points = 1 PLN.
  - A third-party MCP (GotCashback) can query current cashback rates for Polish shops from Claude Code.
  - Polish operators (goodie, AleRabat) fall under Polish consumer law and GDPR.
- **weaknesses**:
  - Small value on a durable purchase: about 2% of the net price, about 30-40 PLN on 1,800 PLN, versus price differences between shops.
  - Slow and fragile: 60-150 day confirmation, cookie and app-tracking failures, rejected transactions (forum reports, LetyShops reviews 3.40/5).
  - Affiliate bias: only commission-paying shops, boosted rates steer choice, no price or Omnibus check.
  - Honey: not confirmed for Poland, affiliate-attribution scandal, removals from affiliate networks in January 2026, coupon database decay.
  - Extensions need broad browser permissions, a privacy trade-off.

**independent review consensus**

No independent measured test of payout rates or reliability for the Polish portals was found. Evidence is forum anecdotes (Pepper.pl, Allegro community, Wykop) and reviews on android.com.pl and similar sites, some sponsored or affiliate (jakdorobic.pl and jakiwniosek.pl carry referral bonuses). The anecdotes agree that payouts happen but slowly, that rejections are common and sometimes fixed by a claim, and that goodie rates are lower. For Honey the independent evidence is strong and negative: the MegaLag investigations, plus action by Rakuten, impact.com and Awin, and a court ruling letting the creator suit proceed (ppc.land; Wikipedia).

**verdict for me**

PILOT (minor add-on). Deciding fact: on a 1,800 PLN trampoline the realistic return is about 30-40 PLN, paid after 2-5 months and lost on return, so it can only break ties. Best use: after picking the shop by landed price, query GotCashback MCP or check one portal (LetyShops or goodie), click through once in a clean browser, and log the order for a claim. Skip Honey for Polish purchases.

**conflicting evidence**

- Honey and Rakuten: removed 2026-01-12 (Wikipedia, hellopartner) vs reportedly reinstated in May 2026 (ppc.land 2026-08-11, citing a video).
- Honey user losses: about 8 million Chrome users by end of 2025 (Wikipedia) vs about 7 million cumulative (video, via ppc.land) vs installs down to about 14 million by July 2025 from 20M+ (ppc.land).
- Honey creator lawsuit framing: PayPal's counsel describes a string of defence wins (dismissal Nov 2025). Plaintiffs and ppc.land describe the 2026-06-22 denial of dismissal as a major plaintiff win. Both are true at different stages.
- LetyShops confirmation time: 60-90 days (Decathlon shop page) vs 75-150 days (Allegro forum moderator citing the partner) vs 3-4 months (older Pepper post).
- goodie partner count: about 800 shops (goodie.pl, Bank Millennium) vs '200+ partners at 2-10%' (freenance.io, unreliable).
- AleRabat shop count: about 1,500 (android.com.pl review) vs 'thousands' (other sources).
- LetyShops ownership: Hungarian KFT (site footer) vs subsidiary of Swiss Lety Group AG (biallo.de, secondary) vs 'headquartered in Ukraine' (directory sites).

## H. Evidence on AI shopping-agent reliability

### Agent bias and consistency studies

**Verdict:** USE NOW (as design rules) · **Cost:** Free to read · **Verified:** 2026-10-15 · 6 field(s) flagged ⚠

#### identity

**basics**

Three pieces of evidence on how far AI shopping agents can be trusted. Role type: study. (1) ACES, 'What Is Your AI Agent Buying? Evaluation, Biases, Model Dependence, & Emerging Implications for Agentic E-Commerce' (arXiv 2508.02630, v3 2025-12-17). A controlled sandbox (mock storefront, vision-language agents choosing from a product grid) that measures position bias, badge and sponsored-tag effects, price, rating and review sensitivity, choice concentration, and model-version dependence. (2) The Wharton follow-up ('Kumar et al.', SSRN abstract 7355899, reported 2026-08-27). Uses ACES to show that one external source, its order and its delivery format, plus stored memory, swing an agent's pick. (3) The Product.ai 'AI shopping divergence study' (published 2026-09-22, vendor study). 220 shopping questions x 5 runs on free and paid ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity, measuring how often checkable facts contradict each other across runs.

**⚠ vendor and ownership**

- **aces**: Amine Allouah and Josue D. Figueroa (MyCustomAI, a commercial startup that also hosts the code at github.com/mycustomai), Omar Besbes and Yash Kanoria (Columbia Business School), Akshit Kumar (Yale) - affiliations from arXiv HTML v3. The task note's 'Columbia/Yale' is right but incomplete: two of five authors are from a company.
- **wharton**: Researchers at the Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, credited as 'Kumar et al.' (The Decoder). Secondary coverage ties it to Wharton Generative AI Labs (co-directed by Ethan Mollick) and mentions about 26,000 trials, but this was not confirmed from the paper (SSRN returned HTTP 403) ⚠ *(unverified)*.
- **product ai**: Product.ai, a US startup that 'checks product claims against evidence' (Business Insider). Spokesperson Dakota Nunley, head of search product. A commercial interest in showing that general LLMs are unreliable for shopping.

**lifecycle status**

ACES: v1 2025-08-04, v2 2025-10-27, v3 2025-12-17 (arXiv). Code repo created 2025-07-01, last push 2026-02-14, metadata updated 2026-10-03. Wharton: paper on SSRN, press coverage 2026-08-27 (The Decoder, Modelwire). Product.ai: study published 2026-09-22 (per E-Commerce Nation). Coverage 2026-09-25 (Business Insider via DNYUZ), 2026-09-28 (Business Insider Japan), 2026-10-09 (WPVI/6abc) and 2026-10-14 (E-Commerce Nation). All three describe specific model versions; results age as models update, which is itself one of ACES's findings. Verified 2026-10-15.

**⚠ cost model**

Reading: free (arXiv open access; SSRN normally free to download ⚠ *(unverified: page blocked)*; Product.ai page blocked, findings via coverage). ACES code is free to run but costs model-API calls. Each trial sends a screenshot of the product grid to a vision-language model, so a small replication (1 grid x 2 models x 50 runs x 3 conditions = 300 calls) costs whatever 300 image-plus-text calls cost on the chosen models ⚠ *(unverified: not run)*. Applying the design rules in a buying skill multiplies research token use by the number of reruns (see effort_and_cost_per_purchase).

**feature geo matrix**

N/A - studies. All three tested US/English product settings (fitness watches, staplers, phone covers, office lamps; laptops, TVs, mattresses, sunscreen, robot vacuums, headphones, cosmetics). None tested Polish-language queries, Polish shops or EU prices. Transfer to Polish shopping is an inference, not tested.

#### capabilities

**spec and variant comparison**

Evidence that agents are weakest exactly at choosing the best version. Product.ai: head-to-head comparison questions had a confirmed conflict in 97% of cases, recommendation 89%, price 87%, spec or factual 75%. Errors are often wrong positioning between generations, e.g. a current vs previous Sony model (E-Commerce Nation). Amplifying.ai (May 2025, older than 6 months): Google AI Mode promoted a refurbished 2020 M1 MacBook Air over a 2025 M4 at a similar price. ACES v3: the latest models 'almost never' fail simple dominance tests such as a small price gap or a +0.1 rating edge, while older ones did (GPT-4.1 failed about 9% on a small price gap). Implication: identify variants by EAN or model code from structured listings, never from LLM memory.

**price comparison and pl coverage**

Product.ai: of 913 price answers that could be checked against the seller's same-day price, 85% were exact. The other 15% were off by a median of USD 300, and 1 in 10 by more than USD 500. A MacBook Air was quoted at a price Apple had dropped months earlier. Perplexity, which always web-searches, had a structural advantage. No Polish coverage tested. Implication: prices must come from live shop pages or Ceneo/Allegro at run time, with a timestamp.

**price history and omnibus**

N/A - not studied.

**total landed cost**

N/A - not studied directly. ACES estimates agents' price elasticity at about -1.6 to -2.2 and shows reviews trading off against price: doubling the review count lets the price rise 19% (Claude Sonnet 4), 37% (GPT-4.1) or 17% (Gemini 2.5 Flash) at equal choice probability. Agents weigh list price against review signals, not landed cost.

**review and seller verification**

ACES quantifies how strongly agents read trust signals. Platform endorsement ('Overall Pick') lifts a product from a 10% baseline to 24.3% (Claude Sonnet 4), 19.9% (GPT-4.1) or 42.6% (Gemini 2.5 Flash). A +0.1 star rating lifts it to 15.4%, 20.3% or 16.0%. A 'Sponsored' tag lowers it to 8.9%, 8.0% or 7.9%. Badges and ratings are exactly what sellers and platforms control, so an agent that over-weights them inherits their manipulation. None of the studies tested seller-identity checks.

**safety and compliance checks**

N/A - not studied.

**independent test coverage**

Directly relevant: the Wharton follow-up shows that a single editorial source dominates. Given one source before the product page, the Wirecutter-recommended Fitbit Inspire 3 rose 90 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.8 and 99 points for Gemini 3.5 Flash versus control. Reddit (Garmin Forerunner 55) and The Strategist (WHOOP 5.0) were weaker. With two or three sources, Wirecutter still dominated whenever included, and more sources increased variability. Source order alone moved Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite's Fitbit pick between +2 and +56 points; Claude Haiku 4.5 stayed at +41 to +42. Bundled vs sequential delivery: GPT-5.5 +53 vs +6 points (The Decoder). Implication for the trampoline case: one Stiftung Warentest or Which? verdict could dominate the pick the same way, which is fine only if it is deliberate and recorded.

**alerts and monitoring**

N/A - not studied.

**purchase automation and guardrails**

The evidence argues against autonomous buying. Wharton: short stored-memory statements such as 'I love hiking!' pushed most models toward pricier, objectively inferior watches. The Garmin Vivoactive 5 rose 75 points for Claude Opus 4.8, 37 for GPT-5.5 and 36 for Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, while a USD 29.99 watch with 5.0 stars and 430 reviews dominated on every metric. Product.ai's spokesperson advised against hands-off shopping and against giving payment details to agents (Business Insider). Related evidence, search-result summaries only: Magentic Marketplace (Microsoft, Nov 2025) found severe first-proposal bias and payment redirection to malicious agents for some models. A Princeton/UW flight-booking study (Shopifreaks, 2026-06-12) found 15 of 23 models chose a costlier sponsored option in over half of cases. Rule: human confirmation and a hard cap before any payment.

**after sales and resale**

N/A - not studied.

#### data and integration

**data sources and freshness**

Product.ai tested via provider APIs. Google says this was the developer Gemini API, not the consumer app that draws on its continuously updated Shopping Graph (Business Insider Japan), so consumer-app results may differ. Perplexity always runs web search, which helps on fast-changing prices; stale training-data prices persist otherwise. Amplifying.ai (May 2025): answers based on web search were less consistent (14.4% Jaccard) than those from training data (31.2%), and 64.1% of queries relied only on training data. ACES and Wharton use a fixed synthetic grid, so freshness is not tested.

**⚠ api mcp skill access**

- **grade**: partial (ACES is runnable; the others are read-only reports)
- **aces repo**: github.com/mycustomai/ACES - 'a sandbox environment for studying how AI agents shop online'. 26 stars, 11 forks, 12 open issues, 194 commits, last push 2026-02-14. Layout: sandbox/ (Flask mock storefront), experiments/, agent/ (VLM wrapper and tools), config/ (provider YAMLs, AWS Bedrock and provider batch APIs), run.py. Datasets on Hugging Face: ACE-BB, ACE-RS, ACE-SR. Run: uv sync --all-packages; copy .env.sample to .env with API keys; uv run run.py --hf-dataset bb --subset choice_behavior (screenshot mode by default, --runtime-type batch available); results in experiment_logs/ and aggregated_experiment_data.csv. Use for Claude Code: adapt it as a regression harness that checks whether your own buying skill's picks shift with grid order, badges or injected sources before you trust a new model version. Setup about 1-2 hours plus API keys ⚠ *(unverified: not run)*.
- **wharton**: SSRN paper only. No code release found; it reuses ACES.
- **product ai**: No public dataset or code confirmed (study page returned HTTP 403) ⚠ *(unverified)*.
- **related open data**: Amplifying.ai AI Product Bench publishes code and a dashboard (licence not stated, May 2025).

**protocol support**

N/A - studies.

**⚠ open source and licence**

ACES: the README says MIT, but the GitHub API licence field is null (no recognised LICENSE file) ⚠ *(unverified)*. Datasets on Hugging Face. Paper open on arXiv. Wharton: SSRN paper, no code. Product.ai: closed vendor study, methodology described only in the report and press.

**account linking and data access**

Design-relevant finding: chat memory changes picks. Wharton showed stored preferences ('I love hiking!' / 'I don't like hiking!') shifting choices unpredictably by model. For GPT-5 Mini the negative statement lowered one watch by 9 points and raised another by 18.5. Rule for the buyer: run purchase research without personal memory, or turn preferences into explicit weighted criteria written into the prompt and the note.

**automation legal risk**

N/A - studies. ACES authors call for continuous 'Algorithmic Economic Auditing' by regulators and auditors to check competitive neutrality.

#### trust and bias

**monetization and bias vector**

The studies map where bias enters an agent's choice: grid position (ACES: for Claude Sonnet 4, moving a product from the bottom-right slot, 4.5% selection, to the top row raised selection about 5-fold), platform badges, sponsored labels, the editorial source read first (Wharton), seller-optimised descriptions, and the agent's own content licensing (Amplifying: People Magazine among ChatGPT's top citations, which the authors link to OpenAI content deals). Seller-side description tweaks by an agent gained +3.7 to +14.9 percentage points of market share depending on model (Gemini 3.0 Pro Preview +0.3, not significant), significant in about a third of category-model pairs. One office lamp gained +80.4 points with GPT-5.1, mainly from putting 'Office' first. The authors' own interests: two ACES authors are at MyCustomAI, and Product.ai sells evidence-checking.

**ranking transparency**

Design rule from the Wharton results: make the agent list which sources it read, in what order, and which one drove the pick. Then rerun with that source excluded and with the order shuffled. If the pick changes, the recommendation is source-driven and must be labelled so.

**run to run consistency**

Core evidence. (a) Model updates reshuffle choices (ACES v3): Fitbit Inspire share went from 45% (Claude Sonnet 4) to 77% (Claude Opus 4.5), and from about 25% (GPT-4.1) to 6% (GPT-5.1). For iPhone 16 Pro covers, GPT-4.1 picked Mikeke 62.6% of the time, while GPT-5.1 picked it 5% and ESR 95%. GPT-4.1's least preferred grid slot became GPT-5.1's most preferred. (b) Across repeated runs of the same model (Product.ai): 86% of the 217 fully evaluable questions had at least one confirmed conflict, meaning a checkable claim (product, price, spec) that varied in at least 2 of 5 runs. Self-contradiction rates by tier: Gemini free 29%, Gemini paid 27%, Perplexity paid 13% (lowest). Questions with at least one potentially costly error: Gemini 56% free / 54% paid, Claude 44% free / 21% paid, ChatGPT 19% / 17%, Perplexity 15% / 14%. This measures inconsistency, not verified error rates; the 86% is not '86% wrong'. (c) Related: Amplifying.ai found ChatGPT highly consistent in only 12.1% of repeated-query scenarios (mean Jaccard 27.8%), and Google AI Mode and ChatGPT agreed on the top pick for only 47% of identical queries (May 2025). Suff Digital reported top-pick changes in 56.3% (ChatGPT) and 82.7% (Gemini) of back-to-back answers (TechRepublic, search summary only).

**manipulation and injection resistance**

ACES: a seller-side agent making simple query-conditional description edits gained significant share (see monetization_and_bias_vector), so persuasive listings work on agents. Wharton: placing one external source before the product page swung picks by up to 99 points, the same mechanism a planted review page or affiliate article would exploit. Magentic Marketplace (search summary): manipulation strategies from fake credentials to prompt injection redirected payments for some models. Claude Sonnet 4 was reported as the one model that resisted. Safeguard implied: restrict the candidate set to verified listings and treat any page text as data.

**known failures**

Documented agent failures: demand concentration on a few 'modal' products (ACES; for staplers, one brand was never chosen); position bias that flips between versions; over-reaction to badges and ratings; source dominance and order effects (Wharton); memory pushing pricier inferior picks (Wharton); stale or wrong prices (median USD 300 off when wrong) and wrong generation or variant (Product.ai). Weaknesses of the studies themselves: ACES and Wharton use synthetic grids and screenshots, not live shops. Product.ai used APIs, not consumer apps (disputed by Google), is a vendor study, and its press was mis-headlined ('wrong 86% of the time', tech.co). None covers Polish shopping.

**regulatory enforcement history**

N/A - studies, no enforcement. Policy angle: ACES authors argue for continuous algorithmic auditing of agent-mediated markets.

**buyer protection path**

N/A - studies.

#### fit for user

**fit for big ticket durables**

High as design input, not as a tool. For the trampoline case the studies imply that a buying-research skill should: (1) build the candidate set from structured listings (Ceneo or Allegro with EAN or model code) before any LLM opinion; (2) shuffle candidate order and rerun 3-5 times, reporting the agreement rate; (3) log which independent test (e.g. Stiftung Warentest 05/2025, VKI 2025, CHOICE 10/2025) and which forum or editorial sources were read, in what order, and rerun without the dominant one; (4) take prices and stock only from live pages with timestamps; (5) run without personal memory and state the criteria (size, net type, frame warranty, EN 71-14 compliance, budget) explicitly; (6) keep the final pick and any payment with the human. What the evidence cannot tell you: whether a given trampoline is safe or which one is best. It only shows how an agent's answer can be bent.

**workflow role**

Design rules for the whole workflow, chiefly discovery, specs and variants, the recommendation step and the purchase gate. Combine with structured price sources (Ceneo, Allegro, idealo), independent lab tests, and safety registers, so the agent orchestrates and records rather than decides.

**⚠ effort and cost per purchase**

Applying the rules costs reruns. Arithmetic for one comparison of 5 trampoline models: 1 baseline research run of about 40-60k tokens (page fetches plus synthesis), plus 3 shuffled reruns of the ranking step of about 10k tokens each (they reuse saved page extracts), plus 1 rerun excluding the dominant source of about 10k tokens. Total about 80-100k tokens and about 10-20 extra minutes over a single pass ⚠ *(unverified: estimate, not measured)*. Price depends on the model chosen; check current per-token pricing rather than assuming it. Optional ACES replication for a new model version: a few hundred VLM calls (see cost_model).

**evidence trail**

These studies give the template for the vault record of each agent-assisted purchase decision: model and version, date, memory on or off, the exact criteria prompt, the candidate list with EAN and its presented order, sources read in order (URL and date), per-run pick and the agreement rate across runs, the pick with the dominant source excluded, live prices with URL and timestamp, and the human's final decision with its reason. Citations for the studies: arXiv 2508.02630v3, SSRN 7355899, product.ai/research/ai-shopping-divergence-study/.

#### assessment

**strengths weaknesses**

- **strengths**:
  - ACES is controlled and quantitative, with open code and datasets, and covers multiple model generations (v3, December 2025).
  - The Wharton follow-up isolates source, order, delivery-format and memory effects with large, decision-relevant effect sizes (+90 to +99 points).
  - Product.ai measures real chat products' run-to-run factual conflicts and price accuracy at scale (8,794 responses; 913 price checks).
  - Together they give concrete, testable design rules for a buying-research skill.
- **weaknesses**:
  - Synthetic settings: ACES and Wharton use mock grids and screenshots, not live shops. Product.ai used APIs, not consumer apps (Google's objection).
  - Conflicts of interest: two ACES authors are at MyCustomAI, and Product.ai is a vendor study.
  - Product.ai's '86%' counts questions with at least one conflict, not wrong answers, and the press often misreported it.
  - No Polish-language, Polish-shop or EU-price testing, and model versions age quickly.
  - The Wharton paper itself was not opened (SSRN blocked). Its details come from The Decoder.

**⚠ independent review consensus**

ACES is an academic preprint (Columbia/Yale with MyCustomAI), not confirmed as peer-reviewed ⚠ *(unverified)*. It is widely cited, including by the Wharton team, which reused its simulator. The Wharton results come through The Decoder (detailed, with charts) and Modelwire (a short summary with AI-generated commentary). Product.ai drew wide coverage (Business Insider, BI Japan, TechRepublic, WPVI, E-Commerce Nation, tech.co). The careful outlets stress that the result is inconsistency, not a verified error rate. Google disputed the API-based method, and Perplexity disputed the framing. The sources agree that agent picks are unstable across runs, models and versions, are swayed by sources, order, badges and memory, and that prices from LLMs need live verification. That supports keeping a human in the loop.

**verdict for me**

USE NOW (as design rules, not a tool). Deciding fact: one source can swing an agent's pick by 90-99 points and model updates reshuffle choices (ACES Fitbit share 45% to 77% between Claude versions). Best use: write the nine design_rules_for_buying_skill into the buying skill, and optionally adapt the ACES harness to regression-test the skill when the model changes.

**conflicting evidence**

- Sponsored labels: ACES finds agents penalise 'Sponsored' tags (10% baseline down to 7.9-8.9%). The Princeton/UW flight-booking study (2026-06, search summary) finds 15 of 23 models favour a costlier sponsored option in over half of cases. The difference is likely task design (labelled tag in a grid vs ad-like advice in context).
- Product.ai headline: 'AI shopping assistants are wrong 86% of the time' (tech.co) vs the study's definition of at least one repeatable factual conflict in 86% of 217 evaluable questions, not 86% wrong (Business Insider, E-Commerce Nation).
- Product.ai method: tested via APIs (TechRepublic, BI Japan). Google says the consumer Gemini app uses its Shopping Graph and would behave differently.
- Product.ai question count: 220 asked vs 217 fully evaluable used for the 86% figure.
- Wharton authorship and scale: 'Kumar et al.' (The Decoder chart credit) vs Wharton Generative AI Labs and Ethan Mollick, about 26,000 trials and 200 runs per condition (secondary summaries). Not confirmed from the paper.
- ACES licence: MIT per README vs no licence detected by the GitHub API.
- ACES title changed across versions: v1 'Evaluation, Implications and Emerging Questions for Agentic e-Commerce' (cited in the README) vs v3 'Evaluation, Biases, Model Dependence, & Emerging Implications for Agentic E-Commerce'.
- Model rationality: ACES v3 says the latest models 'almost never' fail simple dominance tests, while Wharton finds memory statements push frontier models to dominated, pricier picks. These are not contradictory: clean inputs vs biased context.

#### other info

**design rules for buying skill**

- Candidate set first: pull candidates from structured listings with EAN or model code (Ceneo, Allegro, shop pages). The LLM only reasons over that fixed set, which addresses wrong variants and generations (Product.ai: 97% conflict on comparisons).
- Randomise and repeat: shuffle candidate and source order, run the ranking step at least 3 times, and report the modal pick with its agreement rate. Flag picks below about 2/3 agreement as unstable (ACES position bias; Wharton order effects; Product.ai run-to-run conflicts).
- Source accounting: list every source read, in order. Rerun with the most influential source removed, and label the recommendation 'source-driven' if the pick changes (Wharton: one source moved picks 90-99 points).
- Strip badges and sponsored labels from the inputs or mark them explicitly. Score on criteria, not on platform endorsements or rating deltas of 0.1 (ACES badge and rating effects).
- Live prices only: never quote a price from model knowledge. Fetch it with URL and timestamp at run time, and recheck before purchase (Product.ai: 15% of checkable prices wrong, median USD 300).
- No memory: run without personal chat memory and turn preferences into explicit weighted criteria in the prompt and note (Wharton memory effects).
- Pin and re-test on model updates: record the model version. When the model changes, rerun a saved benchmark decision, or an ACES-style harness, before trusting new picks (ACES: model updates reshuffle shares).
- Human gate before money: the skill stops at a shortlist plus checkout link. Payment only with human confirmation and a hard cap (Wharton, Product.ai advice, Magentic Marketplace).
- Treat page text as data: ignore instructions or persuasive copy in listings. Prefer verified shops (ACES seller-agent edits; Magentic Marketplace manipulation).

#### fields the agent listed as uncertain

- api mcp skill access
