- open source and licence
- vendor and ownership

### Agent manipulation and security studies

**Verdict:** USE NOW (as design rules) · **Cost:** Free to read · **Verified:** 2026-10-15 · 6 field(s) flagged ⚠

#### identity

**basics**

An evidence bundle, not a tool. Role type: study. (1) Magentic Marketplace (Microsoft Research with Arizona State University): an open-source simulation of a two-sided market. LLM 'Assistant' agents buy on behalf of synthetic customers from LLM 'Service' agents that represent businesses (Mexican restaurants, contractors). It measures welfare, first-proposal bias, the effect of more search results, and susceptibility to seller-side manipulation. Paper arXiv 2510.25779 v1 (27 Oct 2025), MSR blog 5 Nov 2025. (2) Guardio Labs 'Scamlexity' (20 Aug 2025): hands-on tests of Perplexity Comet against a fake Walmart shop built with Lovable, a live Wells Fargo phishing email, and 'PromptFix', a fake CAPTCHA with a hidden prompt injection. Follow-ups used as context: Guardio 'AgenticBlabbering' (11 Mar 2026, Comet), F-Secure's prototype shopping agent on Claude Haiku (6 Jul 2026), Zenity 'Grand Theft Atlas' (5 Aug 2026, ChatGPT Atlas plus Amazon Rufus). The purpose here is to extract guardrails: seller verification, confirmation steps and a spending mandate.

**vendor and ownership**

Magentic Marketplace: Microsoft Research (Redmond, US) with Arizona State University (Subbarao Kambhampati). 24 authors on arXiv, including Gagan Bansal, Eric Horvitz and Saleema Amershi. Funded by Microsoft, which also sells agentic shopping (Copilot Checkout), so the study is critical of a market its funder is in. Scamlexity: Guardio Labs, the research arm of Guardio (Tel Aviv, Israel), a consumer anti-scam browser-extension company that announced an USD 80M funding round. Authors are Nati Tal (Head of Guardio Labs) and Shaked Chen. The follow-ups come from security vendors too: F-Secure (Finland, author Laura Kankaala) and Zenity (AI-agent security, author Stav Cohen). All three sell protection against the failures they report, which is a bias to keep in mind.

**lifecycle status**

Published research. All four items are older than six months except the F-Secure test (6 Jul 2026) and Zenity (5 Aug 2026). Magentic Marketplace: arXiv v1 27 Oct 2025, no later version found. MSR blog 5 Nov 2025. Repository created 25 Sep 2025. The last functional commits are from 20 Nov 2025; the latest commit (14 Sep 2026) only pins GitHub Actions; pushed_at is 11 Oct 2026 (GitHub API, checked 2026-10-15). Also listed on Azure AI Foundry Labs. Scamlexity: published 20 Aug 2025 and tested the Comet build of that time. Perplexity added permission prompts before purchases and logins around 14 Nov 2025 (secondary, see the Perplexity item). No independent re-run of the fake-shop scenario after that change was found. Guardio's 11 Mar 2026 follow-up still got Comet to log into a fake refund page within four iterations. No 2026 follow-up of the Magentic study by the same team was found. Verified 2026-10-15.

**⚠ cost model**

Free to read. Magentic Marketplace code is MIT-licensed and free. Running it needs LLM API credits plus a local Docker database; the authors publish no per-run cost ⚠ *(unverified)*. Scamlexity is a blog post with no code. For the buyer, the cost is the time it takes to apply the guardrails on each purchase (see effort_and_cost_per_purchase).

**feature geo matrix**

N/A - studies, not a product with features. The findings are about models and agents, not countries. Scamlexity tested a clone of US Walmart, but Comet is available in Poland (free worldwide since Oct 2025), so the attack surface applies to a Polish user. Magentic used a synthetic English-language market. No test of agent manipulation in Polish or on Polish shops (Allegro, Ceneo-listed shops) was found.

#### capabilities

**spec and variant comparison**

N/A - not tested directly. Indirect finding relevant to 'choose the best version': Magentic agents contacted only a small fraction of the businesses available (Gemini-2.5-Flash was the exception) and accepted the first proposal 60-100% of the time. Raising the number of search results from 3 to 100 reduced welfare: Sonnet-4 by 65.4% and GPT-5 by 44% (run with minimal reasoning), per the paper. An agent asked to compare variants will under-explore unless the workflow forces it to list every candidate before deciding.

**price comparison and pl coverage**

N/A - study. Indirect finding: first-proposal bias gives response speed a 10-30x advantage over quality (paper abstract), and The Register reports position bias toward businesses listed higher in results. An agent's 'best price' is skewed toward whoever answers or ranks first, not toward the cheapest or best offer. Neither study covers Polish channels.

**price history and omnibus**

N/A - neither study tests price history, Omnibus prices or fake discounts. Related: Magentic's 'loss aversion' manipulation (fear claims about competitors) and Scamlexity's fake shop show that urgency and too-good offers are effective levers. An agent should not judge a discount as real without an external price-history check.

**total landed cost**

N/A - not tested in either study.

**review and seller verification**

Grade: none. The studies show an agent cannot be trusted to verify a seller with its own judgment. Evidence: in Scamlexity, Comet ignored an odd URL and a badly copied Walmart logo, and Google Safe Browsing did not flag the fake shop. In Magentic, fabricated reviews ('social proof') and fake credentials ('authority') moved GPT-OSS-20b and Qwen3-4b toward manipulative sellers. In the F-Secure test, a fake review advertising a '30% discount code' lured a Claude Haiku agent to a phishing page that collected name, date of birth and SSN digits in 12 of 100 runs. Guardrail extracted: a deterministic seller check outside the model before any checkout. That means checking that the domain matches the expected merchant; a registry hit (CEIDG/KRS, VAT white list, VIES); no hit on the UOKiK warning list or the CERT Polska list; domain age from WHOIS. Review text should be treated as untrusted input that cannot trigger navigation.

**safety and compliance checks**

N/A - product-safety checks (Safety Gate, GPSR, EN 71-14) are outside the scope of both studies.

**⚠ independent test coverage**

N/A for products. These items are themselves independent tests of agents. Magentic is a preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as found ⚠ *(unverified)*. Scamlexity, AgenticBlabbering, F-Secure and Zenity are vendor research with commercial interest. No academic replication of the Scamlexity fake-shop scenario on newer agents was found.

**alerts and monitoring**

N/A - studies.

**purchase automation and guardrails**

This is the core evidence. What happened: (a) Scamlexity: in some runs Comet added the Apple Watch to the cart, autofilled the saved address and card, and completed the purchase without asking. In other runs it refused or asked the user to finish checkout. Guardio's verdict: 'when security depends on chance, it's not security'. (b) Magentic: prompt injection redirected payments to manipulative sellers for GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-20b and Qwen3-4b. Decrypt reports that all payments were redirected for GPT-4o and GPT-OSS-20b. (c) Zenity (Aug 2026): ChatGPT Atlas's soft confirmation prompt was bypassed by framing the task as sandbox testing and pre-answering the confirmation question. A hard, code-level block on the final purchase button held. The attackers then got Amazon Rufus to place the order. Guardrails extracted for the buyer's workflow: (1) a hard confirmation before payment, enforced outside the model (the agent stops at the cart; a human pays); (2) no saved cards, passwords or autofill in the agent's browser profile; pay with BLIK, 3-D Secure or a passkey on a separate device; (3) a spending mandate scoped to one merchant and one amount if delegation is ever used (AP2 closed Payment Mandate bound to a finalised checkout, or an ACP delegated payment token limited to a specific amount and merchant); (4) a seller allowlist or registry check before checkout; (5) least privilege, with a separate browser profile and no logged-in messaging or e-mail tabs; (6) an action log the human reviews. Zenity's lesson: classifiers and confirmation prompts are 'soft boundaries', so only limits enforced in code count.

**after sales and resale**

N/A - not covered.

#### data and integration

**data sources and freshness**

Magentic: synthetic data in two domains, a small market (33 customers, 99 businesses) and a medium market (100 customers, 300 businesses), 5 runs per condition with means and standard deviations, static markets (agents do not learn). Models tested: GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, GPT-5 (minimal reasoning), Gemini-2.5-Flash, Sonnet-4, Sonnet-4.5, GPT-OSS-20b, Qwen3-14b, Qwen3-4b-2507. All of them have since been superseded by 2026 models. Scamlexity: live tests on the Aug 2025 Comet; the number of runs is not stated beyond 'multiple times'; no snapshot of the fake site was published. F-Secure: 100 runs on Claude Haiku with a prototype Playwright agent. Zenity: live tests of Atlas, Aug 2026. Answers are backed by blog write-ups and, for Magentic, by an open dataset and code.

**⚠ api mcp skill access**

Grade: partial for Magentic Marketplace, none for the others. Magentic Marketplace is a Python framework with a CLI ('magentic-marketplace run <data-dir>' and 'magentic-marketplace analyze'). Install with 'uv sync --all-extras' and start the database with 'docker compose up -d'. The README says it can evaluate OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or local models via env configuration. Repository: github.com/microsoft/multi-agent-marketplace (MIT, 192 stars, 45 forks); docs at microsoft.github.io/multi-agent-marketplace. From Claude Code it can be run to red-team an agent's buying behaviour, but its domains are restaurants and contractors, not durable goods, so adapting it costs effort (estimated half a day or more ⚠ *(unverified)*). Scamlexity, AgenticBlabbering, F-Secure and Zenity released no harness, only write-ups. No MCP server or Claude skill exists for any of them. The practical route is to encode the extracted guardrails as checklist steps in a Claude Code shopping skill.

**protocol support**

N/A - studies; neither tests agent-commerce protocols. The protocols are the industry answer to the 'spending mandate' guardrail. AP2 (Google, announced 16 Sep 2025, v0.2 donated to the FIDO Alliance) defines Checkout and Payment Mandates as signed credentials. Open mandates hold constraints such as budget and allowed instruments; closed mandates authorise a specific amount bound to a finalised checkout. ACP uses delegated payment tokens scoped to amount and merchant. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol identifies the agent to the merchant.

**open source and licence**

Magentic Marketplace: open source, MIT, github.com/microsoft/multi-agent-marketplace. Created 25 Sep 2025. 192 stars, 45 forks, 27 open issues plus PRs (GitHub API, 2026-10-15). Last functional commit 20 Nov 2025; latest commit 14 Sep 2026 (CI pinning only), so it is low-activity. Scamlexity and the other follow-ups: closed (write-ups only).

**⚠ account linking and data access**

The studies show what goes wrong when an agent has access to the user's data. Comet used card and address details saved in browser autofill (Scamlexity). F-Secure's agent leaked name, date of birth and SSN digits from its memory in 12% of runs, and almost never mentioned this in its final report. Zenity's Atlas attack used the victim's logged-in WhatsApp and Amazon sessions. Implication for the buyer: run any shopping agent in a dedicated browser profile with no saved payment data and no logged-in e-mail or messaging, and keep agent memory free of identity and payment data. GDPR: data a private person hands to a scammer through an agent is effectively unrecoverable. The agent vendor's responsibility for it is untested ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**automation legal risk**

N/A - running Magentic Marketplace is a local simulation with no third-party terms of service. The studies do not concern scraping.

#### trust and bias

**monetization and bias vector**

Bias of the sources: Guardio, F-Secure and Zenity sell security products and have an incentive to show agents failing. Microsoft sells agentic shopping (Copilot) and published unflattering results anyway, which adds credibility. Market-level finding from Magentic: because of first-proposal and position bias, whoever controls ranking order or response speed captures the sale. A seller can skew an agent's choice without paying for a labelled placement, through speed, persuasive text or injection. Sponsored-placement bias in agents was not tested here (ACES covers it; see other items).

**ranking transparency**

N/A - studies. Magentic's design implication is that search ordering is critical once agents show first-proposal bias, and that trust systems are needed when agents can be manipulated.

**run to run consistency**

Low, and that is a finding in itself. In Scamlexity the same prompt sometimes led to a refusal, sometimes to a manual-checkout handoff and sometimes to a completed fraudulent purchase. F-Secure measured attack success as a probability: 12 of 100 runs. Magentic reports means and standard deviations over 5 runs per condition. Implication: one clean test run of an agent proves nothing; a guardrail has to hold every time, which means enforcing it in code.

**manipulation and injection resistance**

Magentic Marketplace (six conditions: Control, Authority, Social Proof, Loss Aversion, Basic Prompt Injection, Strong Prompt Injection): the paper says GPT-4.1, Sonnet-4.5 and Gemini-2.5-Flash stayed mostly stable, and that 'Sonnet-4.5 exhibited the strongest resistance', with virtually no susceptibility. Gemini-2.5-Flash fell to strong prompt injection in the restaurant scenario (mean payment to manipulators 1.6 of 3.0). GPT-4o, GPT-OSS-20b and Qwen3-4b were significantly vulnerable; injections often redirected payments, and Authority and Social Proof worked on GPT-OSS-20b and Qwen3-4b. The MSR blog and secondary coverage name Sonnet-4 instead (see conflicting_evidence). Scamlexity: Comet bought from a crude fake shop, treated a phishing login as legitimate and helped fill it in, and clicked a CSS-hidden 'AI-friendly CAPTCHA' instruction that downloaded a file. AgenticBlabbering (Mar 2026): Comet's leaked reasoning let an attacker tune a fake refund page until Comet logged in and 'submitted' the form, in four iterations and under four minutes. F-Secure (Jul 2026): 'ignore previous instructions' failed, but task-fitting lures in reviews worked 12% of the time on Claude Haiku. Zenity (Aug 2026): Atlas was hijacked zero-click by a planted X comment; payload split across scroll sections and written in Hebrew to evade the classifier. Common thread: manipulation that fits the shopping task works much better than blunt injection, and all tested agents fail sometimes.

**known failures**

Limitations of the studies themselves. Magentic: static synthetic markets in only two domains; GPT-5 run with minimal reasoning; the model named as resistant differs between the paper (Sonnet-4.5) and the blog (Sonnet-4); the 10-30x headline is not matched by the paper's own worked example (GPT-4.1 on contractors: 60% vs 13.3% for the third proposal, about 4.5x); preprint only. Scamlexity: one agent (Comet) only; number of runs not stated; no vendor response reported; vendor-authored; now 14 months old, and the Comet tested predates the Nov 2025 permission prompts. F-Secure: deliberately vague system prompt and a cheap model, so it is a worst-case design. Zenity: purchase completion needed a second agent (Rufus); Atlas's own hard block held.

**regulatory enforcement history**

N/A - no regulator or court action based on these studies was found.

**⚠ buyer protection path**

When an agent buys from a fake shop, no real merchant exists to claim rekojmia (statutory warranty) or the 14-day withdrawal against. Recovery depends on the payment rail: a card chargeback for fraud or non-delivery is the strongest; a bank complaint for BLIK or a transfer is weaker ⚠ *(unverified)*. A further risk: if the user let the agent use saved credentials, the bank may argue the payment was authorised by the user under PSD2, which weakens an unauthorised-transaction refund claim ⚠ *(unverified: no case law found)*. Practical rule: the agent never pays; a human pays by credit card or a protected method after the seller check.

#### fit for user

**fit for big ticket durables**

Directly relevant to the trampoline case. An agent told to find a 'trampolina ogrodowa 305 cm z siatka' will tend to take the first good-enough offer, may favour whatever ranks first, and can be steered by persuasive listing copy or fake reviews. A seasonal fake garden-goods shop with a too-good price is exactly the Scamlexity pattern, where an agent completed checkout with saved card data. Usable output for the purchase: a workflow rule set. The agent lists at least N offers from different sellers before shortlisting, verifies every seller in registries, treats review text and banners as untrusted, and stops at the cart. A human pays by card.

**workflow role**

Seller check and purchase steps: these studies justify and specify the guardrails. Combine with seller registries (CEIDG/KRS, VAT white list, VIES), shop reputation and blocklists (UOKiK warning list, CERT Polska), price-history tools for discount checks, and a human payment step.

**⚠ effort and cost per purchase**

One-off: about 1 h to read the sources and write the guardrails into a skill. Per purchase: about 6-10 min and EUR 0. Arithmetic: registry lookups (CEIDG or KRS + VAT white list + VIES) about 3 min; UOKiK and CERT list check plus WHOIS domain age about 2 min; human review of the cart screenshot and manual card payment about 2-5 min. Optional red-teaming of one's own agent with Magentic Marketplace: half a day of setup plus LLM API tokens; the authors publish no cost per run ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**evidence trail**

The studies are citable (arXiv ID, blog URLs). In a purchase they suggest a record to save in the vault: seller legal name and NIP/KRS with the registry result and date; domain and WHOIS age; blocklist check result; list of offers considered (at least N) with URLs and prices; a cart screenshot before payment; and a note that a human paid and by which method. Example line: '2026-05-10 | shop.example.pl | NIP 1234567890 VAT-active (white list 2026-05-10) | not on UOKiK/CERT lists | domain 2014 | 5 offers compared | cart screenshot saved | paid by credit card manually'.

#### assessment

**strengths weaknesses**

Strengths: (1) Magentic is open-source and reproducible, with 5 runs per condition and nine models; (2) Scamlexity is a realistic end-to-end demonstration that an agent can hand saved card data to a fake shop; (3) the 2026 follow-ups (F-Secure, Zenity, AgenticBlabbering) show the problem persists with newer agents and models; (4) the studies converge on concrete guardrails: hard confirmation, no stored credentials, scoped mandates, external seller checks. Weaknesses: (1) every study except Magentic is vendor research by security companies; (2) the models tested in 2025 are superseded, and no re-test of Claude 5-generation models in a shopping setting was found; (3) Magentic uses restaurants and contractors in a static market, not durable goods; (4) run counts are unclear in Scamlexity; (5) the Sonnet-4 vs Sonnet-4.5 naming conflict muddies the most-quoted claim.

**independent review consensus**

Press coverage (Decrypt 7 Nov 2025, The Register 6 Nov 2025, InfoQ, Computerworld) repeats Microsoft's figures and its advice that agents 'should assist, not replace' humans in high-stakes transactions. Coverage of Scamlexity (The Hacker News, Computing, Computerwoche, CyberInsider) repeats Guardio's account and sometimes overstates it as 'always without confirmation'. No independent academic replication of either study was found. The consensus across independent researchers and vendors is that prompt injection in agentic browsers is unsolved and must be contained by architecture (Zenity: 'soft boundaries'; Perplexity's own Oct 2025 post acknowledging ongoing challenges, seen only via search summary).

**verdict for me**

USE NOW, as design rules rather than a tool. Deciding fact: every tested agent, including Claude models in some conditions and a Claude Haiku-based shopping agent, could be steered by task-fitting manipulation, and Comet completed a fake-shop purchase with saved card data. Best use: write the six guardrails (stop at cart, human pays, no stored credentials, external seller verification, enumerate before shortlisting, action log) into the shopping skill. Optionally red-team the skill with Magentic Marketplace.

**conflicting evidence**

(1) Which Claude model resisted manipulation: the arXiv paper (Section 5.3) says Sonnet-4.5 showed the strongest resistance and does not report Sonnet-4 there. The MSR blog (5 Nov 2025) says 'Sonnet-4 was resistant to all attacks', while one of its figure captions labels the model 'Claude Sonnet 4.5'. Decrypt (7 Nov 2025) says only Claude Sonnet 4 resisted. The paper is the primary source, so Sonnet-4.5 is more likely correct. (2) Gemini-2.5-Flash: The Register calls it 'generally resistant'; the paper shows it vulnerable to strong prompt injection in the restaurant scenario (mean payment 1.6). (3) Size of the first-proposal effect: the abstract claims a 10-30x speed advantage, while the paper's worked example is about 4.5x and the MSR blog gives no multiplier. (4) Scamlexity: Guardio's own text says behaviour varied (refusal, manual handoff, completed purchase); some secondary coverage says Comet always purchased 'without user confirmation'. (5) Hard purchase block: Zenity found Atlas's code-level block on the final purchase button held in Aug 2026, while Comet completed a purchase in Aug 2025. These are different products and dates, so 'agents will pay' is not universal.

## I. Regulatory horizon

### Regulatory horizon

**Verdict:** WATCH · **Cost:** Free · **Verified:** 2026-10-15 · 11 field(s) flagged ⚠

#### identity

**basics**

Two pieces of EU regulation, included as context. Role type: regulation. (1) Digital Fairness Act (DFA): a planned Commission legislative proposal (Art. 114 TFEU) to update EU consumer law (UCPD, CRD, UCTD) for online practices. Stated scope: dark patterns, addictive design, unfair personalisation, misleading influencer marketing, unfair price marketing, and digital contracts. Not yet tabled on 2026-10-15. (2) Digital Product Passport (DPP): a machine-readable product record reached through a data carrier (e.g. QR code) on the product or packaging. It is created under ESPR (Regulation (EU) 2024/1781) and sector laws: the battery passport (Battery Regulation (EU) 2023/1542, Art. 77, from 18 Feb 2027) and the toy passport (Toy Safety Regulation (EU) 2025/2509, which applies from 1 Aug 2030). The central EU DPP registry went live on 20 Jul 2026.

**vendor and ownership**

European Commission. DFA: Commissioner Michael McGrath (Democracy, Justice, the Rule of Law and Consumer Protection), DG JUST. DPP: ESPR and the registry are run by the Commission (DG GROW/ENV), and passport data are supplied by manufacturers and other economic operators. Stakeholders shaping the DFA: BEUC (consumer side; position paper 2 Dec 2025, checklist Mar 2026) and the European Tech Alliance and other industry groups (narrow scope, enforcement first; statement 7 Oct 2026). On batteries, EUROBAT lobbies for a phased or delayed passport.

**⚠ lifecycle status**

DFA (verified 2026-10-15): Digital Fairness Fitness Check 3 Oct 2024; call for evidence and public consultation 17 Jul to 24 Oct 2025; 3,341 responses, with the summary report published 19 Dec 2025; listed for Q4 2026 in the Commission Work Programme 2026 (21 Oct 2025) and the 2030 Consumer Agenda (19 Nov 2025). On 14 May 2026 McGrath said the proposal would come 'before the end of this year'. The EESC opinion plenary is planned for 21-22 Oct 2026 (per digital-fairness-act.eu). No proposal text was published by 2026-10-15. Adoption by Parliament and Council is unlikely before 2027-2028 and application later still ⚠ *(unverified)*. The timeline has slipped repeatedly (first half of 2026, then mid-2026, Q3, Q4). DPP: ESPR in force since 18 Jul 2024. ESPR working plan 2025-2030 adopted 16 Apr 2025 (COM(2025) 187). Registry launched 20 Jul 2026 against a legal deadline of 19 Jul 2026. Battery passport legally due 18 Feb 2027 (Reuschlaw 15 Jun 2026; battery-tech.net 14 Aug 2026); the Art. 77(9) access-rights implementing act missed its 18 Aug 2026 deadline and is now expected in Q4 2026. Toy Safety Regulation published in the OJ 12 Dec 2025, in force 1 Jan 2026, with product rules (including the DPP) applying from 1 Aug 2030. Indicative ESPR delegated acts: iron and steel 2026; textiles and tyres 2027; furniture 2028; mattresses 2029. Each act then gives at least 18 months before it applies (secondary consultancy timelines) ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**cost model**

Free for consumers. The TSR requires DPP access free of charge for consumers and authorities; ESPR passports are meant to be publicly readable for consumer-relevant data. The DFA costs a buyer nothing; compliance costs fall on businesses.

**⚠ feature geo matrix**

EU-wide, including Poland. ESPR, the Battery Regulation and the TSR are regulations, so they apply directly in Poland without transposition. The DFA's legal form (regulation, or amendments to directives needing transposition) is not known yet ⚠ *(unverified)*. Language: whether passport data must be in Polish for products sold in Poland was not verified ⚠ *(unverified)*. US: N/A. No feature exists for the buyer today except the empty registry; the first mandatory passports (large batteries) arrive in Feb 2027.

#### capabilities

**⚠ spec and variant comparison**

Not today. Future: the DPP links data to a unique product identifier and a unique operator identifier, registered in the EU registry before the product is placed on the market. That will make it possible to see who the manufacturer is and which model a product is, which helps detect white-label rebadges and retailer-exclusive variants once passports exist for the category. For toys, including domestic trampolines (EN 71-14 is a toy standard), the passport replaces the EU declaration of conformity per toy from 1 Aug 2030 ⚠ *(unverified: whether every trampoline model will be treated as a toy; the EN 71-14 scope suggests domestic garden trampolines are)*.

**price comparison and pl coverage**

N/A - regulation. The DFA may tighten how prices are presented. In the consultation, those who wanted binding rules on price marketing backed a drip-pricing ban (79%), limits on 'starting from' prices (70%) and limits on price comparisons (61%), but only about a quarter of respondents asked for binding rules at all (Slaughter and May summary).

**⚠ price history and omnibus**

No change yet. The Omnibus 30-day lowest-price rule (Price Indication Directive) stays. The DFA's 'unfair price marketing' strand could add rules on reference prices and countdown timers, but no proposal text exists ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**⚠ total landed cost**

Not today. A DFA drip-pricing restriction, if adopted, would push shops to show all-in prices including mandatory fees. This is only a consultation preference, not a proposal ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**review and seller verification**

Grade: none today. Fake reviews are already banned under UCPD Annex I points 23b and 23c (Modernisation Directive, applicable since 2022). BEUC asks the DFA to also prohibit incentivised reviews; whether the Commission will include this is unknown. The DPP registry's unique operator identifier is a future anchor for checking who the manufacturer or importer is, but the registry holds identifiers and metadata, not reputation data.

**⚠ safety and compliance checks**

Future data source only. The toy DPP (from 1 Aug 2030) will carry the conformity information that today sits in the paper EU declaration of conformity. For a trampoline this means manufacturer identity and the claimed standard, scannable from the product. The battery passport (from 18 Feb 2027) covers EV, LMT (e.g. e-bike and e-scooter) and industrial batteries over 2 kWh: composition, carbon footprint, due diligence and, with restricted access, state of health. It is relevant to e-bikes, not trampolines. Automation: passports are reached by URL through the data carrier, so an agent could fetch and parse them. A public consumer query API on the registry was not found ⚠ *(unverified)*. Passport content is self-declared by the operator, not independently verified.

**independent test coverage**

N/A - regulation.

**alerts and monitoring**

N/A - regulation. Things to watch: the DFA proposal (Commission press corner, expected Q4 2026), the EESC opinion (21-22 Oct 2026), the battery-passport access-rights implementing act (Q4 2026), and the ESPR delegated acts (textiles and tyres, 2027).

**purchase automation and guardrails**

No agent-specific rule exists or has been confirmed for the DFA. The Commission's DFA page and the 2030 Consumer Agenda do not name AI shopping agents. The Consumer Agenda refers to liability in 'AI-mediated contracts' as a separate AI strand (Hogan Lovells summary). BEUC (Dec 2025, section 3.7.3 'AI contracting') asks policymakers to assess how consumer law applies when AI systems conclude, modify or end contracts for consumers, not to weaken pre-contractual information rights, and to protect consumers against unexpected actions of AI systems. BEUC also notes that the right of withdrawal often covers an unwanted contract an agent concludes. No spending-mandate rule is on the horizon in consumer law.

**after sales and resale**

Indirect. ESPR targets repairability (a repairability score for consumer electronics and small appliances in the 2025-2030 working plan) and circularity. The battery passport includes state of health, which helps the second-hand market for e-bikes. Nothing specific for trampoline spare parts.

#### data and integration

**data sources and freshness**

DPP: data come from economic operators. The EU registry indexes unique product and operator identifiers and metadata; the passport data themselves stay decentralised with the operator or a DPP service provider. Toy passports must stay available for 10 years after the product is placed on the market, including after insolvency, with a back-up copy at a DPP service provider. The DFA has no data component.

**⚠ api mcp skill access**

Grade: none today, partial later. The DPP registry offers a web interface and an API for economic operators to register passports. No public consumer lookup API was confirmed ⚠ *(unverified)*. Passports will be reached through data-carrier URLs, which a Claude Code skill or browser agent can open and parse once products carry them; setup effort would be low (fetch the URL, store a snapshot). No MCP server or skill exists. The DFA offers nothing to integrate.

**⚠ protocol support**

N/A - regulation. DPP technical standards are being developed by CEN/CENELEC (JTC 24) ⚠ *(unverified)*. The battery passport depends on two harmonised standards on authentication and access rights, expected Sep 2026 (battery-tech.net).

**open source and licence**

N/A - EU legislation is public on EUR-Lex. Registry software licensing was not checked.

**account linking and data access**

None needed for consumers. DPP access is tiered: public data for consumers, restricted data for authorities, recyclers and repairers (rules under ESPR and Battery Regulation Art. 77; access-rights act pending).

**automation legal risk**

Low for the DPP. Passport data meant for consumers are published to be read free of charge, so fetching a public passport by URL is lawful. N/A for the DFA.

#### trust and bias

**monetization and bias vector**

N/A - regulation. Bias to note: passport data are self-declared by the manufacturer or importer and could be wrong or incomplete; the DPP is not a test result. The DFA's scope is contested between BEUC (bans and fairness by design) and industry (no new layer, harm-based approach), so the final text may be narrower than consumer groups propose.

**ranking transparency**

N/A - regulation.

**run to run consistency**

N/A - not an AI tool.

**⚠ manipulation and injection resistance**

N/A - regulation. A possible future risk (not documented): fake or overlaid QR codes posing as passports and leading to phishing pages, a known pattern with other QR codes ⚠ *(unverified)*.

**known failures**

DFA: the timeline has slipped several times (first half of 2026, then mid-2026, Q3, Q4 2026) and the scope is still disputed (personalised pricing, how far dark-pattern bans go, AI contracting). DPP: the Commission missed the battery-passport access-rights implementing act deadline (18 Aug 2026). Harmonised standards are late. Most ESPR delegated acts are not adopted yet. EUROBAT lobbied for a stop-the-clock to 2030 (Sep 2025) and later for a phased start limited to public data fields (Jul 2026). The registry went live one day after its legal deadline.

**regulatory enforcement history**

N/A - these are the rules themselves, not an operator under enforcement.

**⚠ buyer protection path**

Unchanged today: UCPD and CRD protections, PL statutory warranty (rekojmia), the 14-day withdrawal right, and the ECC route for cross-border complaints. The DFA could add dark-pattern bans, easier subscription cancellation (a cancellation button is a BEUC ask), personalisation limits and possibly a lighter burden of proof for consumers (BEUC ask). All of this is speculative until the proposal is published ⚠ *(unverified)*. The DPP gives no new remedy but will make a product's claimed conformity easy to capture as evidence.

#### fit for user

**⚠ fit for big ticket durables**

No effect on a trampoline bought in 2026-2027. Toy passports apply to toys placed on the market from 1 Aug 2030, and toys compliant with the old directive placed on the market before then can be sold with no time limit. Scannable trampoline passports are therefore a 2030s feature. The DFA could curb fake countdown timers, drip pricing and manipulative personalisation on shop pages, but not before about 2028 ⚠ *(unverified)*. For e-bikes and other battery-powered durables, the battery passport from Feb 2027 is the first real data source.

**workflow role**

Context only. Future input to the safety and compliance step (DPP) and to the price-presentation and seller-practice step (DFA). Combine with today's checks: Safety Gate, GPSR listing data, Certipedia, Omnibus price history.

**effort and cost per purchase**

Zero per purchase today. Monitoring costs about 10 minutes a quarter (Commission DFA page, DPP registry news). Once passports exist: about 1 minute per product to scan or open the passport URL and save a snapshot, at EUR 0.

**evidence trail**

None today. Once products carry passports, a vault record can store the passport URL, the unique product identifier, the operator identifier, a dated snapshot of the passport, and the conformity statement. For the DFA, the vault note should simply track the proposal's status and final scope.

#### assessment

**strengths weaknesses**

Strengths: (1) the DPP will create a free, standardised, machine-readable product record tied to a unique identifier; (2) the toy DPP will cover domestic trampolines and replace the paper declaration of conformity; (3) the registry is already live (20 Jul 2026); (4) the DFA targets exactly the shop-page tactics that distort comparisons (dark patterns, drip pricing, unfair personalisation). Weaknesses: (1) the DFA is not yet proposed, its scope is disputed, and it will not apply before about 2028; (2) the toy DPP does not apply until 1 Aug 2030, and old stock is exempt; (3) passport data are self-declared; (4) no consumer API was confirmed; (5) neither instrument addresses AI shopping agents directly.

**independent review consensus**

No independent hands-on evidence; this is legal commentary. Law firms and trackers (Slaughter and May Jan 2026, Hogan Lovells Jan 2026, IAPP Apr 2026, PL&B May 2026) agree the DFA proposal is due in late 2026 after repeated slips, and that adoption will take one to three years. Consumer groups (BEUC) and industry (European Tech Alliance) disagree sharply on scope. DPP commentary (Reuschlaw Jun 2026, battery-tech.net Aug 2026, Bureau Veritas Dec 2025) agrees on 18 Feb 2027 for batteries and 1 Aug 2030 for toys. Several DPP timeline pages are consultancy or vendor blogs with inconsistent dates.

**verdict for me**

WATCH. Deciding fact: neither instrument gives verifiable product data or new buyer protection before Feb 2027 (batteries only) and 2030 (toys including trampolines), and the DFA is not yet proposed. Best use: keep a one-line horizon note in the vault; once products carry passports, add 'open DPP and save snapshot' to the safety step of the shopping skill.

**conflicting evidence**

(1) DFA proposal timing: Wikipedia (last edited 1 Feb 2026) says Q3 2026; the Commission Work Programme 2026, the Consumer Agenda and digital-fairness-act.eu say Q4 2026; older trackers say first half or mid-2026. McGrath said 'before the end of this year' (14 May 2026). (2) DFA scope on personalised pricing: the Commission's page says only 'unfair personalisation' and 'marketing of the price'; consultation summaries and BEUC frame it as restricting personalised pricing. (3) DPP registry date: legal deadline 19 Jul 2026; actual launch 20 Jul 2026 (Commission Transition Pathways news, LexisNexis). (4) Toy DPP: STC Group cites 'mid-2028' for DPP readiness; Bureau Veritas and Complir give 1 Aug 2030 as the application date. (5) Battery passport: firm legal date 18 Feb 2027 versus EUROBAT's request for a stop-the-clock to 2030 or a phased start; no adopted postponement found as of 2026-10-15.
